title: Don't Fail to Come: How Burroughs Talked Wellcome Into London
dek: An American selling compressed tablets to London doctors needed help, wrote to an old classmate, and lent him part of his stake; their partnership began in 1880.

story.event: Burroughs persuading Wellcome to join him in London to sell compressed tablets, and the partnership of 1880
story.summary: In 1878 Silas Burroughs moved from Philadelphia to London as agent for John Wyeth & Brother, selling compressed tablets by calling on doctors with free samples. Needing help, he wrote to his fellow Philadelphia graduate Henry Wellcome in 1879, and the two began the partnership of Burroughs Wellcome & Co in September 1880, Wellcome borrowing from Burroughs to buy his share. The firm registered the Tabloid trade mark in 1884 and grew quickly, but the partners fell out; Burroughs failed in 1889 to dissolve the partnership and died in 1895.
paragraphs: In the spring of 1878 Silas Burroughs left Philadelphia for London as sole agent for John Wyeth & Brother. He knew their product well: his pharmacy thesis had been on the compression of medicinal powders, and the Wyeths had been making compressed pills since 1873. They found him wayward and expensive, the historian Roy Church writes, but wanted his knowledge. He was to call on doctors and leave free samples, a practice the Wyeths believed unknown in Britain.

His pitch was that tablets were convenient, exact in dose and "not liable to change by keeping." Persuasion was slow. Burroughs judged that English doctors took time to convince, and feared they linked compressed pills with American quackery, so he called them tablets rather than pills. Good salesmen were hard to find; "we are, therefore, doing it ourselves," he told the Wyeths. In August 1879 he wrote to Henry Wellcome, a fellow Philadelphia pharmacy graduate travelling for McKesson & Robbins in New York: "Our house is the only one in the kingdom calling on doctors with samples of new things."

Wellcome was unsure. According to a 1995 account by William Hoffman, his uncle Isaac, a preacher who kept a small drugstore in Maine, told him to stay in his well-paid job, while the Mayo doctors in Minnesota urged him to go. Burroughs kept writing: "Don't fail to come." Wellcome came. The partnership began in September 1880 with capital of £2,000, and because Wellcome had little money, Burroughs lent him much of his share at ten per cent interest. Even before the deed was confirmed, Wellcome's display at the British Medical Association meeting in Cambridge drew praise in the medical press.

The firm began making its own tablets in 1883 and in 1884 registered the trade mark Tabloid. By 1892, Church records, it employed 600 people. The friendship did not last. In June 1889 Burroughs failed in the High Court to dissolve the partnership, and by the end of that year the two communicated only in writing or through others. Relations were still bitter when he died suddenly in Monte Carlo in February 1895, leaving Wellcome in control of the business.

quote.text: I had an associate, who was for years the companion of my travels, partook of the same bread and salt, and enjoyed the many rights of a confirmed friendship. At last, on some trifling advantage, he gave me cause of umbrage, and our intimacy ceased.
quote.locator: Chapter V, "On Love and Youth", Story XIII
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi's two friends shared bread and salt for years, fell out over a small advantage, and in his telling made their peace. Burroughs and Wellcome's friendship carried their firm through its start, then ended in a lawsuit and written messages, and the peace never came.

reflection: Burroughs wanted Wellcome for what he knew and whom he knew, and he was willing to lend him the money to join. That generosity was real. It also meant the two did not begin as equals, and nothing in the partnership deed could make their tempers match.

Saadi's line is a reminder that friendships between colleagues often break on small things. If you work, or hope to work, alongside people you like, it is worth saying early, while it is easy, how you would part if you ever had to. The point is not to expect an ending. It is that the conversation is kinder now than it would be later.
invitation: If you share work with a friend, ask them one question this week: what would each of us want if this ever ended? Listen, write down the answer, and then let the subject rest.

research_notes: The slate episode ('selling compressed tablets in London') is told through the decision that founded the firm: Burroughs's invitation and Wellcome's choice to accept. Capital: Beckett (2008) quotes Robert Rhodes James that the 1880 deed fixed capital at £2,000, Burroughs £1,200 and Wellcome £800, but that Wellcome could contribute only £400 in cash and borrowed £550 from Burroughs at ten per cent; these figures do not quite add up, so the story says only that Burroughs lent him much of his share at ten per cent. Church and Tansey (quoted by Beckett) say the deed envisaged equal capital by September 1884. Ages differ: Church gives Wellcome as 27 at the invitation, Hoffman 26 in 1880 and Grace's Guide 27, while Grace's gives Burroughs as 35 though he was born in December 1846; the story gives no ages. Hoffman says the firm was 'incorporated' in 1880 and that Wellcome was wealthy by 30 and the drugs 'an instant success'; it was a partnership, and Church describes slower persuasion, so those claims are not used. A Sudan Journal of Paediatrics article (2013) wrongly dates Burroughs's death to 1885 and was not used. Outcome numbers: Church says sales of S M Burroughs & Co in its first year 'may have reached £2,000' (not used, as he hedges it), records 600 employees by 1892 and more than 1,000 by 1901, and BW&Co sales of £575,756 in 1911; the story uses only the 1892 workforce, attributed to Church. Church also notes that compressed medicines of the time 'offered questionable medicinal value but were, at least, harmless'; the story describes the pitch rather than endorsing the products. Wellcome's hesitation and family advice rest on Hoffman's 1995 account alone and are attributed. Manufacturing from 1883 comes from Grace's Guide. The 1894 renewed dissolution talks (Wikipedia) are not used; Beckett supports the bitterness of the last years. Saadi's story is about a personal friendship, applied here by analogy.
